parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what is happening on the surface - light goes in and electrons come out. What is the standard name for light knocking electrons free from a metal?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Light To Electron Release**
You have ultraviolet light hitting magnesium in a vacuum and electrons flying off. This is not reflection or ionisation in a gas. It is the classic evidence for the particle nature of light where one photon gives its energy to one surface electron to release it.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Focus on the words 'at least $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$'. This is the threshold frequency $f_0$ where electrons are just released with zero kinetic energy.
Hint 2: Recall how photon energy links to frequency, then use the threshold frequency to find the minimum energy needed to escape, which is the work function $\Phi$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Understand Work Function**
The work function $\Phi$ is the minimum energy needed to free an electron from the metal surface. At the threshold frequency $f_0$, the incoming photon has just enough energy to do this, with nothing left over for kinetic energy.

Step 2: **Calculate With E = hf**
Use the Planck relation for a photon:
$$E = hf$$
At threshold:
$$\Phi = h f_0$$
$$\Phi = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (8.8 \times 10^{14})$$
$$\Phi = 5.8 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Start from energy conservation - the photon energy splits into the work needed to escape plus the leftover kinetic energy of the electron.
Hint 2: Calculate the new photon energy $hf$ for $f = 11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ and subtract your work function from (b)(i) to get $E_{MAX}$.
Hint 3: Convert that kinetic energy to speed using $E_{MAX} = \frac{1}{2}mv_{MAX}^2$ with electron mass $m = 9.11 \times 10^{-31} \text{ kg}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Apply Einstein Equation**
One photon is absorbed by one electron. Energy is conserved:
$$hf = \Phi + E_{MAX}$$
where $E_{MAX} = \frac{1}{2} m v_{MAX}^2$ is the maximum kinetic energy. Electrons deeper in the metal lose more energy, so this gives the fastest ones.

Step 2: **Find The Leftover Energy**
Photon energy at $f = 11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$:
$$hf = (6.63 \times 10^{-34}) \times (11 \times 10^{14}) = 7.29 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$
Subtract the work function:
$$E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$$
$$E_{MAX} = 7.29 \times 10^{-19} - 5.83 \times 10^{-19} \approx 1.46 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$

Step 3: **Convert Energy To Speed**
$$\frac{1}{2} m v_{MAX}^2 = E_{MAX}$$
$$v_{MAX} = \sqrt{\frac{2E_{MAX}}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \times 1.46 \times 10^{-19}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}}}$$
$$v_{MAX} = 5.7 \times 10^{5} \text{ m s}^{-1}$$

parts.label: (c)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what happens when $f$ is below $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$. Are any electrons emitted and what does that mean for $E_{MAX}$?
Hint 2: Rewrite the Einstein equation as $E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$. What shape does this predict for $E_{MAX}$ against $f$ once emission starts?
Hint 3: Use your answer from (b)(ii) to fix the top end of the line - what is $E_{MAX}$ in units of $10^{-19} \text{ J}$ when $f = 11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$?
parts.proper_answer: $E_{MAX} = 0$ for $f = 8.0$ to $8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$, then a straight line of positive gradient $h$ from $8.8$ to $11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$, reaching $\approx 1.45 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$ at $11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Zero Region Below Threshold**
For $f < f_0 = 8.8 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$ the photon energy $hf$ is less than $\Phi$, so no electrons can escape. Draw $E_{MAX} = 0$ flat along the f-axis from $8.0$ to $8.8$.

Step 2: **Linear Rise Above Threshold**
Above threshold:
$$E_{MAX} = hf - \Phi$$
This is $y = mx + c$ form with gradient $h$ and f-intercept $f_0$. So from $8.8$ upwards draw a single straight line sloping up with constant positive gradient. It must start exactly at the threshold.

Step 3: **Fix The End Point**
From (b)(ii), at $f = 11 \times 10^{14} \text{ Hz}$:
$$E_{MAX} \approx 1.46 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}$$
So on the axis $E_{MAX}/10^{-19} \text{ J}$ the line ends at about $1.45$ when $f/10^{14} \text{ Hz} = 11.0$. Join $(8.8, 0)$ to $(11.0, 1.45)$ with a straight line.
